content: The toothbrush is a tool designed with a small brush attached to a handle, specifically used for cleaning teeth through the process of brushing. Toothpaste, which often contains fluoride, is typically applied to the toothbrush to enhance its cleaning effectiveness. Toothbrushes are available in a variety of bristle textures, sizes, and shapes. Most dental professionals, including the American Dental Association, recommend using toothbrushes labeled as soft, as firmer bristles can potentially damage tooth enamel and irritate the gums. Modern toothbrushes are commonly made from synthetic fibers, although natural toothbrushes are still used in some parts of the world. The first commercially produced toothbrush was invented by Goldstein and Hautman in 1875. History Oral hygiene practices have been in existence since prehistoric times, as evidenced by archaeological findings worldwide. Items such as chew sticks, tree twigs, bird feathers, animal bones, and porcupine quills have been recovered from ancient sites. The earliest concept of a modern toothbrush is believed to have originated in China during the late 1400s. These early toothbrushes were made using stiff hog neck hairs attached to bamboo sticks. However, other cultures also developed their own versions of toothbrushes. For instance, ancient Indian medicine utilized the neem tree and its derivatives for oral hygiene, while in the Muslim world, the miswak (or siwak), a twig or root with natural antiseptic properties, was widely used. Additionally, substances like baking soda and chalk were commonly rubbed against teeth for cleaning. William Addis of England is credited with creating the first mass-produced toothbrush in 1780. While imprisoned in 1770 for inciting a riot, he sought to improve the contemporary method of cleaning teeth, which involved rubbing a rag with soot and salt on the teeth. He crafted a toothbrush by drilling holes into a small animal bone, threading bristles obtained from a guard into the holes, and securing them with glue. This innovation led to his financial success, and upon his death in 1808, he passed the business to his eldest son, William II. The first toothbrush patent in the United States was granted to H. N. Wadsworth in 1857 (U.S. Patent No. 18,653). However, mass production of toothbrushes in America did not begin until 1885. Early designs featured bone handles with holes for Siberian boar hair bristles. Boar hair, however, was not an ideal material as it retained bacteria, dried poorly, and often shed bristles. The widespread adoption of toothbrushes in the United States was partly due to their inclusion in the daily hygiene routines of American soldiers during World War II, a habit they continued after returning home. In 1938, DuPont replaced natural bristles with synthetic fibers, specifically nylon, revolutionizing toothbrush design. The first nylon-bristled toothbrush, made with nylon yarn, was introduced to the market on February 24, 1938. The first electric toothbrush, the Broxodent, was launched by the Bristol-Myers Company (now Bristol-Myers Squibb) in 1959 during the centennial celebration of the American Dental Association. In January 2003, the toothbrush was recognized as the most indispensable invention by Americans, surpassing the automobile, computer, cell phone, and microwave oven, according to the Lemelson-MIT Invention Index. Electric Toothbrushes The first electric toothbrush was developed in Scotland in 1939 but did not become commercially available until the 1960s, when it was marketed in the United States as the Broxodent by Squibb. In 1961, General Electric introduced a rechargeable cordless toothbrush that moved in an up-and-down motion when activated. By 1987, the first rotary-action toothbrush for home use, the Interplak, became available to the general public. Today, numerous models of electric toothbrushes with various mechanisms are widely available.
